[PATH:empirical] World Values Survey (WVS) wave 6-7, combined with OECD GDP per capita data and Gini coefficients for OECD countries (2010-2020) — Provides individual-level data on subjective well-being and social comparison attitudes among high-income earners, enabling cross-national correlation analysis with GDP per capita and inequality measures to test the hypothesized negative relationship.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal panel studies on income rank and social comparison (e.g., German Socio-Economic Panel, SOEP) with focus on top-income deciles — Allows tracking within-country changes in social comparison frequency over time for high-income earners, controlling for GDP growth and inequality shifts, to establish causal direction and rule out confounds.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical literature on 'positional externalities' and 'Easterlin paradox' (e.g., works by Robert Frank and Richard Easterlin) applied to high-inequality contexts — Offers a framework linking higher GDP per capita to reduced marginal utility of income and increased relative deprivation concerns, predicting amplified social comparison among the rich in unequal societies, which could refute or refine the hypothesis.

C006.subject: GDP per capita
C006.object: self-reported mental health outcomes among high-income demographics in countries with high economic inequality
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP per capita self-reported mental health outcomes among high-income demographics in countries with high economic inequality]

[PATH:empirical] World Happiness Report microdata (2010-2023) for OECD countries with Gini > 0.4, stratified by income quintile — Directly tests the correlation between GDP per capita and self-reported mental health (e.g., Cantril ladder, negative affect) among top-income respondents, controlling for individual-level income.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review of the 'Easterlin Paradox' and income-mental health link in high-inequality contexts (e.g., Wilkinson & Pickett, The Spirit Level, updated with 2010-2023 data) — Provides theoretical grounding and existing evidence on whether higher national income benefits only the wealthy when inequality is high, or if relative deprivation dampens the effect.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal cohort study (e.g., German Socio-Economic Panel or UK Understanding Society) comparing mental health trajectories of high-income individuals in high- vs. low-inequality regions — Allows within-country analysis over time, isolating the effect of aggregate GDP changes on high-income mental health while controlling for individual income and regional inequality.

C007.subject: GDP per capita
C007.object: self-reported mental health outcomes among high-income demographics in countries with strong social safety nets
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP per capita self-reported mental health outcomes among high-income demographics in countries with strong social safety nets]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal panel data from the OECD's Better Life Index, stratified by income quintiles and controlling for Gini coefficients, to compare GDP per capita trends with self-reported mental health scores (e.g., Cantril ladder or WHO-5) among high-income respondents in countries like Denmark, Norway, and Sweden. — Provides direct, time-series evidence on the correlation within the specified demographic and safety-net context, while controlling for income inequality as required.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of studies using the 'Easterlin Paradox' framework, focusing on high-income groups in welfare states, to test whether diminishing marginal utility of income leads to negative mental health associations (e.g., through social comparison or status anxiety). — Synthesizes existing findings to assess whether the hypothesized negative correlation holds across multiple datasets and theoretical models, addressing the disputed status.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical model based on 'relative deprivation theory' and 'social safety net crowding-out effects,' simulating how increased GDP per capita might reduce social cohesion or increase individualistic stress among the affluent in strong safety-net systems. — Offers a causal mechanism to explain the proposed negative correlation, enabling targeted empirical tests and refinement of the hypothesis.

C008.subject: GDP per capita
C008.object: self-reported mental health outcomes among high-income demographics in countries with strong social safety nets
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP per capita self-reported mental health outcomes among high-income demographics in countries with strong social safety nets]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal analysis of the European Social Survey (ESS) data, focusing on self-reported mental health (e.g., WHO-5 index) and household income quintiles within high-income groups across OECD countries with strong social safety nets (e.g., Denmark, Sweden, Norway) post-2008. — The ESS provides repeated cross-sectional and panel data that can directly test the correlation between GDP per capita and mental health among high-income respondents in strong safety-net contexts, controlling for confounders like unemployment and inequality.

[PATH:literature] Review of the 'Easterlin Paradox' literature and recent updates on subjective well-being and income, particularly studies by Kahneman and Deaton (2010) and subsequent replications focusing on high-income thresholds in welfare states. — This hypothesis challenges the standard diminishing-returns model; a targeted review of studies on satiation effects, social comparison, and status anxiety in affluent contexts can clarify whether negative correlations are robust or artifacts of measurement.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical modeling of 'relative income' and 'aspiration treadmill' effects using agent-based simulations calibrated to OECD data on income distribution and mental health prevalence. — The hypothesis implies mechanisms such as status competition or hedonic adaptation that may be amplified in high-income groups; formal modeling can test whether these mechanisms produce a negative correlation under strong safety-net conditions.
